source: original; stimulus paraphrased from the 1965 education and housing laws

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the 1965 education and housing laws, from the grounding books. The Department of Housing and Urban Development was created by a separate law, the Department of Housing and Urban Development Act, P.L. 89-174, September 9, 1965.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the Great Society's education and housing laws of 1965. The Elementary and Secondary Education Act sent federal grants to schools in poor areas of the country. The Higher Education Act gave federal aid to college students from low-income families. Head Start, begun in 1965, prepared disadvantaged preschool children for school. The Housing and Urban Development Act of 1965 funded housing and urban improvements, and a separate law that year created the Department of Housing and Urban Development to supervise them.

stem: Taken together, the education and housing laws in the passage best show that the Great Society attacked poverty by

options.text: giving cash directly to every poor adult
options.misconception: The passage lists grants, student aid, preschool, and housing, not cash to every poor adult.

options.text: moving poor families to the countryside
options.misconception: The passage improves schools and cities where people live; it does not move families to the countryside.

options.text: cutting all federal spending on cities
options.misconception: The passage says the housing law funded improvements for cities, so spending rose, not fell.

options.text: improving poor people's surroundings: schools, housing, and cities

rationales.A: The passage lists grants, student aid, preschool, and housing, not cash to every poor adult.
rationales.B: The passage improves schools and cities where people live; it does not move families to the countryside.
rationales.C: The passage says the housing law funded improvements for cities, so spending rose, not fell.
rationales.D: The laws touch schools, colleges, preschool, housing, and whole cities, so they improve the conditions around poor people.
rationales.general:
1. The education laws reach children at three ages: preschool, school, and college.
2. The housing law reaches homes and whole cities.
3. None of these laws hands out cash; each one improves a condition of daily life.
4. The Great Society therefore attacked poverty by improving the conditions around poor people.
Remember: A set of laws shows its aim when you list what each one touches.
